name: Carla Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Carla, thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties, and we don't campaign for anything. What you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say out loud and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay, good. I've done a couple of surveys before but they were all tick boxes. This sounds more like a chat.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: It is. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do interior fit-out, mostly drywall and partitions, for a firm that does refurbishments in hospitals and schools. At the moment we're turning an old ward at the district hospital into outpatient clinics, so it's metal studs, plasterboard, door frames, a lot of fiddly work around pipes and cables. The best part is when the boards are up and a big empty shell suddenly looks like rooms. The worst part is working round the hospital: we start at seven, we can't make noise during certain hours, and we're up and down ladders in dust masks all day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Marco drives the number 14 bus, so between his shifts and mine it's a juggling act getting Giulia and Teo to school. Giulia's fourteen and thinks I'm embarrassing, Teo's ten and still thinks it's cool that his mum builds walls. We've got about three months' money in the bank, give or take, which feels like a lot until the car needs tyres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. On our sites the big tech thing was meant to be the scanning and the 3D models, and half the time the drawings still don't match what's behind the old walls. I'd probably post something sarcastic in the crew chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means not much. I use one of those chat apps now and then to help me write emails to the school office about Teo, or to check a measurement conversion, and that's about it. If that's all it ever is, fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. I'd finish the hospital job and go where the firm sends me next. Marco and I talked about me doing my supervisor ticket in a year or two, and I'd probably still go for that, just for the bump in pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, even, like the news cycle wore me out over nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the drawings not matching.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month we opened up a wall on the old ward, and the 3D model said it was clear. Behind the plaster was a cast iron pipe nobody had on any plan, probably from the 1960s. The model was lovely, all colours, and completely wrong. My foreman Dev just laughed and said, there's your artificial intelligence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that world you'd want to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The same things as now, really. The hospital's short of money, so jobs get cut back halfway through and we get laid off for a couple of weeks between contracts. That's not about AI, that's about how we pay for public buildings. I'd still be going on about that at union meetings.

S0.say: Honestly I'm not surprised AI turned out to be mostly hype. On our sites the fancy scans and 3D models still miss half of what's behind the old walls.
S0.think: For me it means very little. I use a chat app now and then for emails and conversions, and if that's all it ever is, I'm fine with that.
S0.do: Finishes the hospital fit-out and moves to the firm's next refurbishment. Still plans to take her supervisor ticket in a year or two for the extra pay.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit flat, as if the news wore her out over nothing.
S0.quote: The model was lovely, all colours, and completely wrong.
S0.fieldNote: Carla is a light, practical user of AI with no strong feelings about it. Her real frustrations are funding gaps and layoffs between public contracts. The pipe story shows a grounded scepticism about tech on refurbishment sites. Nothing in this picture threatens her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to make sure the gains get shared. If machines are doing more of the boring jobs, fine, but the workers should get the time back or the money back, not just the owners. I'd say that at the union and I'd probably share articles about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think drywall is one of the easier bits to automate on new builds. Big flat walls, standard boards. Refurbs are messier, so I'm a bit safer, but I'm not stupid. The bread-and-butter work goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools more on purpose, not just for emails. I'd ask Dev if I can help with the digital site plans, so I'm the person who knows both the tools and the walls. And I'd push the union branch to get training paid for by employers, not out of our own pockets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit like when you hear a creak above you in an old building. Probably nothing, but you listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the tools more on purpose. What would that look like on a Monday morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take photos of a room, ask the app to help work out the board count and the cuts, then check it against my own numbers. If it's right three times out of four, I'd start trusting it a bit. My sister-in-law already does that for her kitchen fitting and she says it saves her an hour a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Giulia about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's already asking what she should do after school. I'd tell her to pick something where she works with people and also understands the machines. And I'd tell her not to listen to her mum too much, because I'm figuring it out as I go too.

S1.say: If machines take over more of the boring work, the workers should get the time or money back, not only the owners. I'd say that at the union and share it online.
S1.think: I think drywall on new builds is one of the easier things to automate, with big flat walls and standard boards. Refurbishment is messier, so I'm safer, but the bread-and-butter work goes first.
S1.do: Starts using AI tools deliberately for board counts and cut lists, checking them against her own figures. Asks her foreman to involve her in digital site plans and pushes the union branch to get employers to pay for training.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a creak above you in an old building.
S1.quote: Refurbs are messier, so I'm a bit safer, but I'm not stupid. The bread-and-butter work goes first.
S1.fieldNote: Carla responds with a measured, practical plan rather than alarm. She wants proof before trusting the tools and borrows ideas from people close to her, like her sister-in-law. Her politics shape her public line about sharing gains. Her advice to her daughter is modest and honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need strong public support, and fast. Something like a basic income, and the companies using the robots paying a lot more tax. I'd be at the union rallies and I'd be writing to our local representative, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd be scared, honestly. Marco's bus would be driving itself by then too, so it's not just me, it's both incomes at once. That's the bit that turns my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop all extras straight away, no takeaways, Giulia's dance classes on hold, which she'd hate me for. Every spare bit goes into savings so we get from three months to six if we can. I'd join every union push for a wage guarantee, and if the jobs disappear I'd apply for whatever public support there is, and lean on my mum, who's offered to have the kids after school to save us childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Not panicking yet, because we'd have a bit of savings and some time, but lying-awake frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first if it gets tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the credit card, which I hate saying. The mortgage is the last thing I'd let slip, because the house is the kids' whole world. Then it's the car, we could manage with one if Marco's working from the depot. Phones, subscriptions, all that goes before the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both incomes at once. Have you and Marco ever talked about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, not seriously. We joke about the bus driving itself. I think if this were real, that's the conversation I'd dread most, sitting at the kitchen table with the bank statements out. He's proud, Marco, he'd take it harder than me.

S2.say: This is exactly why we need strong public support fast, like a basic income and much higher taxes on companies using robots. I'd be at the rallies and writing to my local representative.
S2.think: I'd be scared, because Marco's bus would be driving itself by then too. It wouldn't just be my job, it would be both our incomes at once.
S2.do: Cuts all extras immediately, including takeaways and her daughter's dance classes, and pushes savings from three months toward six. Joins union campaigns for a wage guarantee, applies for public support if the jobs go, and accepts her mother's offer of after-school childcare.
S2.feel: Frightened and losing sleep, though not panicking yet because of the savings.
S2.quote: Marco's bus would be driving itself by then too, so it's not just me, it's both incomes at once.
S2.fieldNote: The double hit to both partners' jobs is what drives her alarm here. Her politics make public support feel like a right, not a shame. She has thought carefully about which bills go first, and protecting the house for the children is the line she holds. The conversation with her partner is the one she dreads most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set this up properly, so let's not waste them like we wasted the warning about housing. Proper retraining, paid for by the companies. I'd be saying that at every union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a chance. I'd be 48. Not ideal, but not too late to move into something nearby, like site safety or inspections, where there's still a person who has to sign things off, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for the site safety course in the evenings, the union often helps pay for those. We'd put an extra 100 a month into savings. I'd keep using the AI tools at work to learn how the new robots are being planned in, and I'd still do my supervisor ticket. Marco would look at retraining too, maybe as an engineer at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I've got a list, and a list makes me feel better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why safety and inspections?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone always has to be the person who says it's safe to go in. My cousin Sara is a building inspector, and she says the paperwork's getting automated but the walking round and signing still isn't. It might go too, eventually. But it's a step, not a leap, and I'm a step person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets harder about having five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Deciding when to jump. With two years, you just react. With five, every month you're thinking, is this the moment I move, or am I panicking early? I'd want to wait until a couple of friends had done the course and liked it.

S3.say: We've got five years to set this up properly, so let's not waste them. Companies should pay for proper retraining, and I'd say so at every union meeting.
S3.think: Five years gives me a chance, even at 48. I could move into something close by, like site safety or inspections, where a person still has to sign things off for a while.
S3.do: Signs up for an evening site safety course in the first year, ideally with union help on the fees, and adds about 100 a month to savings. Keeps learning how robots are planned into jobs and still takes her supervisor ticket, while her partner looks at retraining at the bus depot.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, and having a list helps.
S3.quote: It might go too, eventually. But it's a step, not a leap, and I'm a step person.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turn fear into a plan built from small steps. Carla wants proof from people she knows, such as her cousin, before committing. She names the new worry of timing the jump. Her retraining choice stays close to her trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly if we start now: shorter weeks, retraining, a fair share of what the machines earn. I'd say it to anyone, and I'd vote for whoever has a real plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm 53. That's long enough for me to get properly into inspections or teaching apprentices, and for Giulia and Teo to get through school. It doesn't make it go away, but I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the supervisor ticket first, then the safety course, then maybe an assessor qualification so I could teach at the college. We'd keep saving steadily, nothing dramatic. And we'd talk to the kids about their choices, maybe put a bit aside for Giulia to do a course that isn't the first one everyone's rushing into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than worried. Like a long drive where you know the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said teaching apprentices. Would there be apprentices, if robots do the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good question, and I don't know. Maybe for a while there'd be people learning to work with the robots, fixing them, checking them. I'd be the one who knows what a straight wall looks like. After that, I honestly can't see that far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Teo in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he's got time. He's ten, he loves taking things apart. I'd tell him to keep doing that, because whoever fixes the machines will be busy. And I'd tell him his mum's going to be fine, which with ten years I'd actually believe.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do this fairly if we start now, with shorter weeks, retraining and a fair share of what machines earn. I'd vote for whoever has a real plan.
S4.think: At 53 I'd have time to get properly into inspections or teaching apprentices, and the kids would get through school. It doesn't make it go away, but I can breathe.
S4.do: Takes her supervisor ticket first, then a safety course, then possibly an assessor qualification to teach at the local college. Saves steadily and puts a little aside so her daughter can choose a less crowded course.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful than worried, like a long drive on a road she knows.
S4.quote: And I'd tell him his mum's going to be fine, which with ten years I'd actually believe.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Carla becomes the most hopeful she's been in the interview. Her plan is a ladder of qualifications rather than one big move. She admits she can't see past the point where robots do most of the work. Her advice to her son is warm and practical.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because Marco and I would both be out at once with two kids and a mortgage. What would help is a proper safety net that kicks in fast, and retraining paid by the companies, with wages while you do it, so you're not choosing between learning and eating.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about women on sites. It took me years to get taken seriously, and now everyone's saying the robots will even it all out. Maybe. Or maybe it'll just be the same blokes running the robots. I'd like someone to keep an eye on that.

headlineQuote: Retraining paid by the companies, with wages while you do it, so you're not choosing between learning and eating.
portrait: Carla is a 43-year-old drywall and fit-out worker on hospital and school refurbishments, with a bus-driver partner, two children and about three months of savings. She uses AI now and then and treats it as a tool to be tested, not trusted. She stays calm in the mild pictures, but the fast AGI picture alarms her because both household incomes could vanish together. With more warning time she builds a step-by-step plan toward safety, inspection and teaching work. Her politics make her push for companies to pay for retraining and public support.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and her partner could both lose their jobs at once while they still have two children and a mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A safety net that kicks in fast, and retraining paid for by companies with wages during the training.
